plain: This is where you write the instructions the computer later executes. Think of a restaurant kitchen: on the counter is what you're preparing, to one side the pantry with ingredients organized, and below the stove, where the actual cooking happens. Here the counter is the text you write, the pantry is the list of your files on the left, and the stove is a small window at the bottom where you give the computer orders by typing them. All in one window, so you're not jumping between programs.

account.free: Completely free: $0, no account, no card. You can sign in with a Microsoft or GitHub account if you want your settings to follow you to another computer, but it's optional and doesn't change anything about what the program does. What does cost money are some AI assistants that install inside it: GitHub Copilot has a limited free plan (about 2,000 autocompletes and 50 chat messages a month) and its paid plan runs about $10 a month.
steps: Go to code.visualstudio.com. In the center there's a big blue button that says 'Download for Windows' and it auto-detects your system. It's about 100 MB. Only download it from that domain: search engines carry fake copies that bundle ads and worse into the installer.
Install and check a box that will save you time

Open the downloaded file and click Next until you reach the 'Select Additional Tasks' screen. Check the box 'Add Open with Code action to Windows Explorer directory context menu'. From then on you can right-click any folder on your computer and open it here instantly.
Open a folder, never a lone file

First create an empty folder, e.g. Documents\projects\vscode-practice. Then, inside the program: 'File' menu and then 'Open Folder'. You'll get the question 'Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder?'. If you created the folder yourself, click 'Yes, I trust the authors'. If someone else sent it to you, click 'No' and you'll be able to read it without anything inside it running.
Learn the left column: the explorer

It's the list of your folders and files. Opened with the icon at the very top that looks like two sheets of paper, or with Ctrl+Shift+E. At the top you'll see your folder's name in capitals. Hovering over that row shows four small icons: the first, a sheet with a plus sign, creates a new file; the second creates a folder.
Open the order window: the terminal

'Terminal' menu and then 'New Terminal'. A panel opens at the bottom with a line starting with your folder's address, something like PS C:\Users\your-name\Documents\projects\vscode-practice. Type dir and hit Enter: it lists what's inside. The official shortcut is Ctrl+backtick, but on many keyboard layouts it often doesn't respond, so use the menu and don't waste your afternoon.

Icon of four squares in the left sidebar, or Ctrl+Shift+X. Type in the search box and click the blue 'Install' button. Before installing, check two things on the listing: who publishes it (Microsoft and well-known editors carry a blue verification badge) and the download count. One with 3,000 downloads and a publisher you don't recognize is not the one you want.
account.warning: The terminal isn't a simulation or a practice exercise: every command you type there really happens to your computer, and what gets deleted from there doesn't go to the recycle bin, it's gone. Never paste a command copied from a forum, a video, or a chat without understanding what it does, no matter how convincing whoever gave it to you sounds. And when you open a folder downloaded from the internet, that question about whether you trust the authors is serious: answering yes lets whatever's inside run just by opening it.

first: Create an empty folder in Documents and call it vscode-practice, no spaces or accents in the name: it saves you weird failures later.
Open it with 'File' and then 'Open Folder', and answer that yes, you trust the authors. Its name should appear at the top, in the left column.

Set it to your language if you want: Ctrl+Shift+P, type display language, choose 'Configure Display Language', select your language, and agree to restart. Practical note: almost all tutorials are in English, so a lot of people deliberately leave it in English so the names match.
Create a file with the sheet-with-plus icon, name it notes.txt, type two words inside, and hit Ctrl+S. Look at the tab at the top before and after saving: the white circle disappears.
Open the terminal from the 'Terminal' menu, type dir, and hit Enter. If notes.txt shows up in the list, the terminal is working inside your folder. That's exactly what you wanted to check.
words: The program where you write and save the instructions the computer later reads. What it produces is plain, ordinary text files; the editor just colors them so your eye can follow along better.
The list of folders and files in the left column. It's the same content you'd see opening that folder on your desktop, but pinned next to what you're writing.
The panel at the bottom where you give the computer orders by typing them with the keyboard, instead of clicking. You type a line, hit Enter, and it answers with text.
An add-on you install inside so the program knows how to do something it doesn't out of the box: understand another language, put the menus in your language, warn you of errors as you write.
The folder that contains everything for a specific job. When you open it as a whole, everything else refers to it: what you see on the left, what search finds, and where the command panel starts.
A search box for everything the program knows how to do. Opened with Ctrl+Shift+P, you type a couple of words of what you want and it offers it, without going through the menus one by one.
A file's mailing address: the list of folders you have to go through to reach it. For example C:\Users\ana\Documents\vscode-practice\notes.txt.

When you write something and haven't saved it yet, a filled-in white circle appears in the tab at the top instead of the close X. That circle means what's on screen and what's saved on disk are no longer the same.
matters: Always open the whole folder, not a lone file. Otherwise search won't find any of your other files, the terminal starts in your personal folder instead of your project, and any AI assistants you install inside won't see the rest of the work, so they answer you with things that don't fit what's in front of you.
Save with Ctrl+S before running anything. The computer reads what's saved on disk, not what's on your screen. Without that habit you'll spend half an hour chasing a bug you'd already fixed.

Check the start of the terminal's line before giving a command: it tells you which folder you're in. If it says C:\Users\your-name and you thought you were in your project, everything you install or create ends up in the wrong place and you'll go crazy looking for it.

Install few extensions and always check who publishes them. An extension runs with your same permissions and can read everything in the open folder, including access keys you keep in configuration files. Ten random extensions in your first week means ten programs from strangers inside your computer.
ignore: The little branches icon (Source Control, version control). Used for saving a project's history and being able to go back. You'll want it, a lot, but it really pays off once you have something worth having history for.
Color themes and icon packs. Change the theme if it's tiring your eyes and get back to your work. No theme writes code for you.

The little triangle-and-bug button (Run and Debug). Used to freeze a program mid-run and look inside at its values. Early on, having the program write messages to the terminal teaches you just as well.

questions.prompt: You have a folder on the Desktop called bakery-web with three files inside. You open VS Code and drag one of them into the window. The file shows and edits perfectly, but the left column stays empty, search finds no trace of the other two files, and when you open the terminal, the line starts with C:\Users\your-name instead of bakery-web.

options.text: You've opened a lone file, not the folder. Close that and use 'File' then 'Open Folder' on bakery-web.
options.why: The program uses the open folder as its reference point for everything: that's where the left-column list comes from, that's where search looks, and that's where the terminal starts. With a lone file there's no reference folder, so the terminal falls back to your personal folder. The nuance that makes this the right answer: the file shows and edits beautifully, which is why everything looks fine except for a few loose details.

options.text: The install got stuck halfway; you need to uninstall and reinstall VS Code.
options.why: It's the first thing anyone thinks when half the screen seems broken, and an empty column really does look like a failed install. It breaks the moment you try it: you reinstall, drag the same file, and see exactly the same thing. It's not a fault, it's the normal behavior when no folder is open.

options.text: You're missing an extension that turns on the file list and search.
options.why: It sounds logical because almost everything here is expanded with extensions, and it's easy to assume the basics are too. But the file list, search, and terminal come built in and are in fact working right now: the problem isn't a missing piece, it's that nobody's told them which folder to work on.

questions.explain: This doesn't work on files, it works on an open folder: if you don't tell it which one, everything else fires blind.

questions.prompt: You change a line, switch to the terminal, run it, and the program behaves exactly like before the change. You go back to the editor and notice the tab at the top: where there's usually an X to close, there's a filled-in white circle instead.

options.text: The file isn't saved. Press Ctrl+S and run it again.
options.why: The white circle means exactly that: what's on screen and what's saved on disk no longer match. And the terminal reads the disk, never your screen. The nuance: the editor shows you your changes even if they're not saved, which is why you'd swear you've already changed it.

options.text: The program has an old version stuck in memory; close VS Code and reopen it.
options.why: In many programs restarting fixes oddities, and here it would even work by accident, because closing would ask if you want to save. It breaks in two places: if you click 'Don't Save' on that prompt you truly lose the change with no way back, and the problem reappears the moment you edit the next line.

options.text: You've edited a different file from the one the terminal runs.
options.why: This really does happen, especially with two similarly named files in different folders, and it's worth checking the full path shown above the editor. But the clue is right in front of you here: that white circle only shows up when the file you're looking at has unsaved changes.

questions.explain: White circle in the tab: your change exists only on screen, and the computer keeps reading the old version until you hit Ctrl+S.

shortcuts: Ctrl+Shift+P — the command palette

It's the search box for EVERYTHING the program knows how to do. A box opens at the top, you type what you want in your own words ('terminal', 'language', 'format') and the options show up. If you can't remember where a menu was, don't hunt for it: open this and type. It's the shortcut to learn first; the rest are optional.
Ctrl+P — jump to a file by name

Type three letters of the file's name and hit Enter. Once your project has forty files, this replaces scrolling up and down the left list hunting with your eyes. Trick: type a colon and a number (e.g. :120) and it takes you to that line.
Ctrl+S — save

While a file has unsaved changes, its tab at the top shows a white circle instead of an X. That circle is cause number one of 'I changed the code and nothing's happening'. Save and the circle disappears. Ctrl+K then S saves all open files at once.
Ctrl+Shift+F — search the ENTIRE project

Normal Ctrl+F searches within the open file. This one searches every file in the folder at once and lists where each result shows up. It's how you find 'where on earth is that text that's showing on screen written'.
Ctrl+B — hide and bring back the left column
When the text feels cramped, hide the file list and get half a screen back. One more press and it's back. Sounds trivial and gets used fifty times a day.
'Terminal' menu → 'New Terminal' — open the command window

The official shortcut is Ctrl+backtick, but on many keyboard layouts that key often doesn't respond. Don't waste your afternoon: use the menu. To close it, use the trash icon in its corner, not the X (the X only hides it).
Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z — undo and redo

Undoes the last thing you typed, even if you've already saved. Important warning: this does NOT undo what an AI assistant did across several files at once, nor does it recover a deleted file. That's what Git is for, which is the real undo.
Ctrl+D — select the next occurrence of the same text

You select a word, hit Ctrl+D, and the next matching one gets selected too. Again and the next one. Type once and change all of them at once. Great for renaming something repeated without missing any.
Alt+Up / Down arrow — move an entire line
Moves the line your cursor is on up or down without cutting or pasting. With Shift added (Alt+Shift+arrow) it duplicates it. Used constantly for reordering.
Ctrl+Shift+X and Ctrl+Shift+G — extensions and version control

The first opens the add-ons store. The second opens the Git panel: the list of everything you've changed since the last saved version, with a button to commit it. That second panel is your safety net.
daily: Open folders, not lone files. 'File' → 'Open Folder'. Open a lone file and the terminal won't know where it's working, the AI won't see the rest of the project, and Git won't work. 90% of the weird early hiccups come from this.
Notice the white circle on the tab. Change made but not saved = the computer is still reading the old version. Before saying 'it's not working', check the tabs at the top and hit Ctrl+S.

Read the line where the terminal starts. Before typing any command, look at what's at the start of the line: it's the folder you're in. If it's not your project, the command will run somewhere else. Change it by typing cd and the path.

Copy the whole error, not a summary. When something fails in the terminal, select from the first red line to the end and paste it to the AI exactly as is. 'It's giving me an error' can't be fixed; the fifteen ugly lines can.

Use the Git panel before touching anything major. Ctrl+Shift+G, type a short phrase ('before changing the design'), and click the commit button. That's a save point you can return to even if everything else blows up.

Install very few extensions. With your language set (optional), one for auto-formatting, and your AI assistant's, you're set. Every extra extension is more memory, slower startup, and one more surface for a stranger's code to get in.

Search with Ctrl+Shift+F instead of trying to remember. When you see text on screen and don't know which file it comes from, copy it and search the whole project. It takes you to the exact line in two seconds.

templates.name: The settings that remove half the early-days scares
templates.what: This is a file called settings.json that lives inside your project and tells the editor how to behave in THAT folder: to autosave, to format code on save, not to hide important files, and not to change line endings (the reason a project works on your computer and fails on someone else's). Set it once per project and never think about it again.
templates.how: 1) In the left column, with your project open, create a folder called .vscode (yes, with the dot in front). 2) Inside it, create a file called settings.json. 3) Paste the content below. 4) Save with Ctrl+S. 5) Close and reopen the folder to see it applied. If any of this feels like too much effort, paste the whole block to the AI and say: 'create this file in my project'.
fill: files.autoSave
afterDelay saves one second after you stop typing. If you'd rather control it yourself, set it to off and use Ctrl+S
editor.formatOnSave
true tidies and aligns the code every time you save. Needs a formatting extension installed (Prettier for web, Black for Python)
files.eol
\n is Linux's and servers' line ending. Keeping it fixed stops Git from marking a file as 'changed' when you haven't touched it
editor.tabSize
2 spaces for web (JavaScript, HTML, CSS), 4 for Python. If you work with Python, change it
terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.windows
PowerShell is standard on Windows. On Mac or Linux delete this whole line
files.exclude
What you DON'T want to see in the left-hand list. Note: hiding it doesn't delete it, it just stops getting in the way
templates.code:
{
  "files.autoSave": "afterDelay",
  "files.autoSaveDelay": 1000,
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "editor.tabSize": 2,
  "editor.wordWrap": "on",
  "files.eol": "\n",
  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
  "files.insertFinalNewline": true,
  "terminal.integrated.defaultProfile.windows": "PowerShell",
  "explorer.confirmDelete": true,
  "explorer.confirmDragAndDrop": true,
  "files.exclude": {
    "**/node_modules": true,
    "**/__pycache__": true,
    "**/.DS_Store": true
  },
  "search.exclude": {
    "**/node_modules": true,
    "**/dist": true,
    "**/package-lock.json": true
  }
}

templates.name: The empty project folder, set up right from minute zero
templates.what: Four files created before writing a single line of code that save you from the two classic disasters: accidentally publishing your passwords online, and coming back to the project three months later with no memory of how to start it. Works for any project: a website, a script, or an automation.
templates.how: 1) Create a folder with a short name, lowercase, no spaces or accents. 2) Open it with 'File' → 'Open Folder'. 3) Create these four files with the sheet-with-plus icon. 4) Fill in the README with two sentences; you'll thank yourself later. 5) IMPORTANT: check that .gitignore exists BEFORE uploading anything online. 6) .env.local is the only one carrying real passwords, and the only one that never leaves your computer.
fill: .gitignore
The list of what NEVER gets uploaded. If this line is missing, your keys end up public
.env.example
The key names, no values. It's the shareable copy
.env.local
The real keys. This file stays on your computer forever
README.md
What this is and how to start it. Two sentences are enough
templates.code:
# ─── FILE 1 · .gitignore ───────────────────────────────────
# Everything here NEVER gets uploaded to the internet.
node_modules/
dist/
build/
__pycache__/
.venv/
.env
.env.local
.env*.local
*.log
.DS_Store
.vscode/settings.json


# ─── FILE 2 · .env.example ─────────────────────────────────
# The names, no values. This one DOES get uploaded.
OPENAI_API_KEY=
DATABASE_URL=
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000


# ─── FILE 3 · .env.local ───────────────────────────────────
# The real values. This one NEVER gets uploaded.
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-put-your-real-key-here
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/mydb
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000


# ─── FILE 4 · README.md ────────────────────────────────────
# Project name

What it does, in one plain-person sentence.

## How to start it

1. Copy .env.example to .env.local and fill in the keys.
2. Install what's needed:  npm install
3. Start it:  npm run dev
4. Open it at:  http://localhost:3000

## Where to get each key

- OPENAI_API_KEY: platform.openai.com → API keys
- DATABASE_URL: given to you by your database service

errors: 'code' is not recognized as an internal or external command

You're trying to open the editor by typing code in the terminal and the computer doesn't know what that is. It means that during install, the 'add to PATH' checkbox wasn't checked. Fix it without reinstalling: open the editor by hand, press Ctrl+Shift+P, type 'shell command', and choose 'Install code command in PATH'. Close the terminal and reopen it: until you reopen it, it still won't know.
Cannot load the file ...ps1 because running scripts is disabled on this system

Windows ships with script execution blocked by default, and npm is one. Shows up the first time you try to use npm in the editor's terminal. Fix it: open PowerShell as administrator (right-click the icon → 'Run as administrator') and type: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned. Confirm with Y. Close and reopen the editor. You're not lowering the whole computer's security: you're only allowing signed scripts or ones made by you, under your user.
The term 'npm' / 'python' / 'git' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet

The program isn't installed, or it's installed but the terminal can't find it because it was opened before installing it. First try, free: close the editor entirely and reopen it. The terminal inherits the system's program list at startup, so one just installed won't show up until you restart. If it's still the same after restarting, it isn't installed: go to nodejs.org, python.org, or git-scm.com depending on the case.
Restricted Mode / 'Do you trust the authors of the files in this folder?'

Not an error: it's the security question when opening a folder. While it's in 'Restricted Mode' you can read files but nothing runs, and extensions and the terminal are hobbled. If you created the folder yourself, click 'Yes, I trust the authors'. If you downloaded it from the internet, leave it restricted until you've checked what's inside. Change it later in 'File' → 'Manage Workspace Trust'.
Git not found. Install it or configure it using the 'git.path' setting

The version control panel (Ctrl+Shift+G) can't find Git. Almost always it isn't installed: go to git-scm.com, install it with the default options, and restart the editor. If you do have it installed and it's still complaining, you installed it after opening the editor: restarting fixes it.
I changed the code and nothing changes on screen

Three causes, in this order. One: you haven't saved — check if the tab has a white circle and press Ctrl+S. Two: you edited a file with the same name but in a different folder; check the full path by hovering over the tab. Three: the browser is showing you the version it has cached; reload with Ctrl+Shift+R, which ignores that cache.
Delete `CR` · eslint(prettier/prettier) on every line of the file

Your file has Windows line endings and the project expects Linux ones. Nothing serious, but it fills the screen with red. Fix it once and for all: bottom right, in the blue bar, you'll see 'CRLF'; click it and choose 'LF'. Save. To stop it happening again, leave "files.eol": "\n" in the project's settings.json.
Extension host terminated unexpectedly / the editor is running very slow

Almost always an extension, and almost always the last one you installed. Check without deleting anything: Ctrl+Shift+P → 'Extensions: Disable All Installed Extensions'. If it runs smoothly, turn them back on three at a time until you find the culprit. The other usual cause is having a huge folder open with node_modules inside; adding that folder to files.exclude and search.exclude fixes it.

prompts.name: Set up the project folder from scratch, without knowing how to code
prompts.prompt: Act as the technical person helping me out. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn: I tell you what I want and you create and write the files. I work in Visual Studio Code, on [WINDOWS / MAC], and I have an empty folder open. I want to set up the project skeleton properly from minute zero. Do this in order, one at a time, waiting for me to confirm before moving on to the next. First, ask me up to three questions to understand what I want to build, and don't ask me for technical decisions: ask about the outcome, not the technology. Second, tell me what you're going to install, how much space it takes, whether it's free, and what would happen if I didn't install it; if there are two options, pick one yourself and explain in one sentence why that one. Third, create the folder and file structure for me, including mandatorily .gitignore, .env.example, and a README explaining how to start this, and show me the folder tree drawn out before creating anything. Fourth, give me the terminal commands one at a time, and after each one tell me exactly what text should appear if it went well and what text means it failed. Fifth, once it's set up, tell me the single command I need to type every time I sit down to work. Rule you can't skip: if at any point you're going to create a file containing a password or a key, warn me first and check with me that file is in .gitignore. What I want to build is: [DESCRIBE IT IN ONE SENTENCE].

prompts.name: Explain what this file does and what I can touch without breaking it
prompts.prompt: I'm going to paste a file from my project. I don't know how to code, so I don't want a theory lesson: I want to know what it does and how far I can meddle. Answer me with this exact structure. One: what this file does, in two sentences, as if explaining it to someone who's never seen code. Two: who calls it and who it calls, meaning which other files in my project depend on this one; if you can't tell from what I've pasted, tell me which file you need to see. Three: a list of the parts I can safely change (text, colors, numbers, addresses), with the line number and what would happen if I change it. Four: a list of the parts I should NOT touch and why they'd break. Five: if there's anything in this file that's a security problem, a password written in plain text, or something that'll fail when I publish, tell me first, even if I haven't asked. Six: if anything in this file is written in an outdated way or there's a simpler way to do the same thing, tell me, but don't change it yet. The file is: [PASTE THE FILE].

prompts.name: Fix a terminal error I don't understand
prompts.prompt: I got an error in Visual Studio Code's terminal and I don't know what it means. I'll paste it below in full, without trimming anything. Don't give me theory and don't make me choose between technical options: tell me what to do. Answer me like this, in this order. One: what happened, in one plain sentence. Two: whether this is my fault, something missing that needs installing, a missing key, or a bug in the code that's already written. Three: whether it's dangerous or just annoying, meaning whether there's any risk of losing work while this doesn't work. Four: the solution in numbered steps, telling me literally what to type or where to click, without assuming I know how to open things. Five: after each step, what should show up if it worked. Six: how I stop this from happening again. If you need to see a file from my project to be sure, ask me for it before proposing anything instead of guessing; I'd rather answer a question than get a blind fix. I'm on [WINDOWS / MAC]. What I was trying to do was: [WHAT YOU WERE TRYING]. The error is: [PASTE THE ENTIRE ERROR].

prompts.name: Set up the editor once so it stops getting in my way
prompts.prompt: I want to set up Visual Studio Code once and for all and never think about it again. I don't know how to code and I get lost among the thousand settings. Give me a minimal setup and justify each line. One: give me the complete content of the .vscode/settings.json file for my project, with a comment next to each setting explaining what it does and what I'd notice if I removed it. Two: tell me which extensions to install, four max, and for each one: exact name as it appears in the search box, who publishes it, what problem it solves for me, and whether it's free. Don't recommend any extension with few downloads or from a publisher I don't recognize. Three: tell me which popular extensions NOT to install yet and why they're a distraction while I'm learning. Four: tell me the five keyboard shortcuts I'll actually use every day, and warn me which ones don't work well on my keyboard layout. Five: tell me how to carry this same setup over to another computer without repeating the whole process by hand. I work on [WINDOWS / MAC] and my project is [WEB / PYTHON / AUTOMATIONS].
